bib.title: Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners

read.skipped: References skimmed only; Appendix D full model outputs read but not itemised.

question: Can an LLM be prompted to self-generate relevant exemplars (and knowledge) for each problem so that it reasons better than with 0-shot CoT or fixed labeled few-shot CoT, without labeling or retrieval?
hypothesis: Prompting LLMs to recall relevant problems and solutions in context, as humans do by analogy, makes them perform in-context learning on tailored exemplars and so solve new problems better.
contributions: Analogical prompting: self-generated exemplars and self-generated knowledge + exemplars in a single prompt
Gains over 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench
Analysis of generation vs retrieval of exemplars and of base model scale

method.summary: A single prompt instructs the LLM to recall K relevant, distinct problems with solutions (optionally preceded by a tutorial on core concepts), then solve the target problem in the same pass. Compared with 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, fixed few-shot CoT and retrieved few-shot CoT on math, code and BIG-Bench tasks with GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM 2 and text-davinci/curie models.
method.task: reasoning prompting: math word problems, competitive-programming code generation, BIG-Bench reasoning

datasets.name: GSM8K
datasets.split: test set implied; train set used for few-shot and retrieved exemplars

datasets.name: Codeforces level-A problems
datasets.split: published Jan-Aug 2023, statement within 2000 GPT-3.5-turbo tokens
datasets.source: scraped from codeforces.com; public tests plus hidden tests from result pages, truncated hidden tests skipped

datasets.name: BIG-Bench: word sorting, logical deduction five objects, temporal sequences, reasoning about colored objects, formal fallacies
datasets.source: Srivastava et al., 2022; Suzgun et al., 2022

other.note: used only in the scale analysis (Table 4) and text-davinci-003 in Table 1

other.use: encodes problem statements for retrieved-CoT baseline, cosine similarity

inference.decoding: sampling; temperature 0 for GSM8K, MATH, BIG-Bench; temperature 0.7 for Codeforces
inference.samples: Math and BIG-Bench: one output per problem at temperature 0. Codeforces: 10 outputs per problem, whole evaluation run twice and averaged. No seeds or variance reported.
inference.prompting: Single prompt: problem, instructions to recall K distinct relevant problems (Q/A with answer in \boxed{}), then solve the initial problem. K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench; Codeforces uses a tutorial plus K=3 exemplars, with knowledge before exemplars. text-davinci models get an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars. Baselines: 0-shot; 0-shot CoT ('think step by step'); few-shot CoT with K=5 train exemplars (GSM8K, MATH) or K=3 hand-annotated exemplars (others); retrieved CoT top K=5.
inference.retrieval: Baseline only: Sentence-BERT encodings, top K=5 train problems by cosine similarity

parameters.diversity_instruction: problems must be distinct from each other and from the initial problem

other.cost: more output tokens than 0-shot CoT; fewer input and more output tokens than few-shot CoT (Sec 8)

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of problems answered correctly (GSM8K, MATH, BIG-Bench)

metrics.name: Acc@k (k=1,10)
metrics.definition: whether at least one of k sampled outputs passes all test cases

eval.protocol: Single run at temperature 0 for math and BIG-Bench with no variance or significance test; Codeforces averaged over two evaluations. No test of statistical significance is reported.

availability.data: Codeforces collection procedure described in Appendix B; release not stated

prompts.text:
Your task is to tackle mathematical problems. When presented with a math problem, recall relevant problems as examples. Afterward, proceed to solve the initial problem.
# Initial Problem:
[problem]
# Instructions:
Make sure to include all of the following points:
## Relevant Problems:
Recall three examples of math problems that are relevant to the initial problem. Note that your problems should be distinct from each other and from the initial problem (e.g., involving different numbers and names). For each problem:
- After "Q: ", describe the problem
- After "A: ", explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{}.
## Solve the Initial Problem:
Say "Let's solve the following math problem." Then formulate your response in the following format:
Q: Copy and paste the initial problem here.
A: Explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{} here.

## Analogous Problems:
Offer five diverse examples of math problems that are relevant or analogous to the initial problem. For each problem, elaborate on the solution and conclude with the ultimate answer (enclosed in \boxed{}). For each problem:
- After "Q: ", describe the problem
- After "A: ", explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{}.
## Solve the Initial Problem:
Q: Copy and paste the initial problem here.
A: Explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{} here.
prompts.where: Appendix D.2 (preamble: 'Your task is to tackle mathematical problems...' as D.1)

prompts.text:
Your goal is to write Python3 code to solve competitive programming problems. Given a problem, explain the core concepts in it and provide other relevant problems. Then solve the original problem.
# Problem:
[problem]
# Instruction:
## Algorithms:
Identify the core concepts or algorithms used to solve the problem.
## Tutorial:
Write a useful tutorial about these algorithms.
## Example Problems:
Provide three examples of relevant competitive programming problems that involve these algorithms. For each problem, describe the problem, explain the solution in detail, and then write the correct Python3 code.
## Python3 code to solve the original problem:
Include the following points in your response:
- Explanation of the solution:
- Python3 code to solve the problem:

Your task is to tackle reasoning problems. When presented with a problem, recall relevant problems as examples. Afterward, proceed to solve the initial problem.
# Initial Problem:
[problem]
# Instructions:
Make sure to include all of the following points:
## Relevant Problems:
Recall three examples of problems that are relevant to the initial problem. Note that your problems must be distinct from each other and from the initial problem. For each problem:
- After "Q: ", describe the problem
- After "A: ", explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{}.
## Solve the Initial Problem:
Say "Let's solve the following reasoning problem." Then formulate your response in the following format:

A: Explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{} here.

evidence.quote: We let LLMs self-generate K =5 exemplars for GSM8K and K =3 exemplars for MATH and BIG-Bench tasks.

results.claim: Self-generated exemplars beat 5-shot CoT on GSM8K with GPT-3.5-turbo by about one point.
results.setup: GSM8K, GPT-3.5-turbo, temperature 0, K=5 self-generated exemplars vs 5-shot CoT (K=5 from train set), single run, no variance reported
results.table: Table 1, row Ours: Self-generated Exemplars, column GSM8K GPT3.5-turbo (5-shot CoT row: 76.7%)

results.claim: On GSM8K with PaLM 2 the gain over 5-shot CoT is one point.
results.setup: GSM8K, PaLM 2 (PaLM 2-L), temperature 0
results.table: Table 1, row Ours: Self-generated Exemplars, column GSM8K PaLM2 (5-shot CoT: 80.7%)

results.claim: On MATH with GPT-3.5-turbo self-generated exemplars beat 5-shot CoT by 2.4 points.
results.setup: MATH, GPT-3.5-turbo, temperature 0, K=3 self-generated exemplars; 5-shot CoT uses K=5 from MATH train set
results.table: Table 1, row Ours: Self-generated Exemplars, column MATH GPT3.5-turbo (5-shot CoT: 34.9%)

results.claim: On MATH with PaLM 2 the gain over 5-shot CoT is 0.5 points.
results.setup: MATH, PaLM 2, temperature 0, K=3
results.table: Table 1, row Ours: Self-generated Exemplars, column MATH PaLM2 (5-shot CoT: 34.3%)

results.claim: text-davinci-003 GSM8K: 61.0% vs 54.0% 5-shot CoT, but the davinci rows used an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars.
results.setup: GSM8K, text-davinci-003, temperature 0; the dagger says for text-davinci models an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars was used, the other models got none
results.quote: †For text-davinci models, we use an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars. For the other models, we do not.
results.note: Table 1 prints 61.0%; Table 4 prints 61% for the same cell.

results.claim: Average accuracy gain over 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT across tasks and base LLMs.
results.setup: GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces, 5 BIG-Bench tasks; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, PaLM 2; how the average is computed is not stated
results.quote: achieving an average accuracy gain of +4%

results.claim: Codeforces with GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: knowledge + exemplars reaches Acc@1 15% vs 11% for 3-shot CoT.
results.setup: Codeforces level-A 2023 problems, 50 problems, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, 10 samples at temperature 0.7, evaluated twice and averaged
results.quote: With our prompting method, GPT3.5-turbo achieves competitive performance with GPT4, with a 15% Acc@1 compared to GPT4’s 16% Acc@1.
results.note: The 15% is for self-generated knowledge + exemplars; exemplars alone give 13%. The 16% GPT4 figure is 0-shot and 0-shot CoT.

results.claim: Codeforces with GPT-4: knowledge + exemplars Acc@10 37% vs 31% for 3-shot CoT.
results.setup: Codeforces, 50 problems, GPT-4, 10 samples at temperature 0.7
results.table: Table 2, row Ours: Self-generated Knowledge + Exemplars, column GPT4 Acc@10 (3-shot CoT: 31%)

results.claim: Self-generated exemplars alone on Codeforces GPT-3.5-turbo-16k do not beat CoT at Acc@10 (25% vs 27%); knowledge is what adds the gain.
results.setup: Codeforces, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, exemplars only vs 3-shot CoT and 0-shot CoT (both 27%)
results.table: Table 2, row Ours: Self-generated Exemplars, column GPT3.5-turbo-16k Acc@10

limits: Authors: more inference computation, since more tokens are generated than 0-shot and 0-shot CoT; fewer input and more output tokens than few-shot CoT.

Authors: self-generation can fail if the LLM is weak or has not learned related problems; the method suits stronger or larger models. With text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001 labeled few-shot CoT is better.
Authors: sensitive to specific prompt phrasing (Jiang et al., 2020).
Main results are single temperature-0 runs with no variance or significance test; GSM8K gains over 5-shot CoT are about 1 point.
Codeforces has only 50 problems (two evaluations averaged); Acc@1 differences of 1-4 points correspond to 0.5-2 problems.
Table 1 mixes protocols: text-davinci rows use an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars, other models do not.
Per-task K differs (5 GSM8K, 3 MATH) and K was tuned on GSM8K/MATH with GPT-3.5-turbo (Table 5).
The qualitative analysis shows that even with relevant correct exemplars the model failed 28 of 50 incorrect cases (generalization gap, overreliance).
Model versions (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 June-September 2023) are API snapshots and have dated; code and release of the Codeforces set are not stated.
